results.reader_title: When can the social value of health data research justify weaker consent?
results.reader_what: Argues weaker consent standards require genuine involvement and control for people whose health data is used.
results.reader_why: Sets an ethical condition for opt-out data reuse under the European Health Data Space.
results.reader_more: Data-intensive health research strains traditional informed consent because of the number of contributors and data points, open-ended questions and repeated or secondary use. The paper examines three distinct roles claimed for social value: preventing research waste and setting priorities, justifying risk to participants, and lowering consent standards. The authors argue that if social value is invoked to justify lower consent standards, then meaningful involvement and control must be available to data contributors or their representatives. The argument is conceptual rather than empirical and is set against moves towards opt-out systems, including in the European Health Data Space.

deep_analysis.research_question: What roles the concept of social value can legitimately play in justifying consent standards for data-intensive health research.
deep_analysis.main_finding: Social value cannot on its own justify lowering consent standards; doing so requires an appropriate form of meaningful involvement and control for data contributors.

results.reader_title: How the EU reconciled its openness and digital sovereignty stories

results.reader_more: The article studies the stories the European Union tells about governing digital technology, using the strategic narratives approach. It contrasts an older digital connectivity narrative, which promotes collaboration, engagement and market inclusion, with a newer digital sovereignty narrative that stresses European digital industry, diversified supply chains and less reliance on outside powers. The authors track how both narratives changed as geopolitical competition intensified. They find a point of convergence in the mid-2020s at which the EU appeared to reconcile openness with autonomy. results.reader_title: Europe first small-firm R&D subsidy raised firm performance, and funding not labels did it
results.reader_what: Quasi-experimental study finds EU SME Instrument grants sizeably improved firm outcomes, with private returns comparable to US benchmark.
results.reader_why: Provides causal evidence that EU grant money, not prestige labels, helps small innovative firms.
results.reader_more: The study exploits the sharp scoring cut-off used to award the Small and Medium Enterprise Instrument, the first European research and development subsidy aimed at small firms. Comparing firms just above and just below the threshold gives credible causal estimates across many countries and sectors. Grants produced sizeable improvements across a range of firm-level outcomes, with patterns consistent with the money easing financial constraints. Firms that received only a quality stamp without funding showed no improvement, so the effect comes from the cash rather than the signal. Estimated private returns are positive and comparable to the United States Small Business Innovation Research programme, with spillovers in the form of more new firm entry.

deep_analysis.research_question: What causal effect European R&D grants to small firms have on firm outcomes, and whether certification alone matters.
deep_analysis.main_finding: EU R&D grants to small firms caused sizeable performance gains that came from the funding itself rather than from certification, with returns comparable to the US SBIR programme and positive spillovers on entrepreneurial entry.
deep_analysis.method_or_basis: Publisher abstract on the JRC Publications Repository landing page supplied in the package
deep_analysis.qualification: Effects are identified around the award threshold, so they apply to marginal applicants rather than to all firms.

results.reader_title: How generative AI changes platform power, compared across the US, EU and China
results.reader_what: Comparative institutional analysis finds fragmented AI governance: US market-led, EU process accountability, China industrial promotion with content control.
results.reader_why: Positions the EU AI Act and Digital Services Act as one of three competing governance logics.
results.reader_more: The article argues that generative artificial intelligence turns platform media from systems that curate attention into systems that produce, rank and authenticate synthetic meaning. It links this to lower marginal costs of content, users supplying cognitive data and labour, and growing platform control over what public knowledge appears credible. The method is qualitative comparative institutional analysis using a ten-dimension interpretive codebook, not a quantitative regulatory index. The United States favours innovation, market experimentation and after-the-fact remedies; the European Union builds process accountability through the AI Act and Digital Services Act; China combines industrial promotion with content security and administrative compliance. Platform behaviour is read as minimising compliance costs under fragmented rules.

deep_analysis.research_question: How generative AI reshapes platform media as cognitive infrastructure, and how three jurisdictions govern that shift differently.
deep_analysis.main_finding: The three jurisdictions follow distinct institutional logics rather than converging, and platform strategy is best explained as compliance-cost minimisation under regulatory fragmentation rather than deliberate evasion.

results.reader_title: National AI strategies in Europe mostly ignore the civil servants who must use AI
results.reader_what: Most EU national AI strategies say little about civil servants, and diverge from EU-level upskilling guidance.
results.reader_why: Weak workforce planning limits public administrations ability to deploy AI they already fund.
results.reader_more: The study analyses how EU Member States treat the civil service workforce in their national artificial intelligence strategies. It uses content analysis and cluster analysis, then compares national approaches with guidance from EU institutions. Most strategies give limited attention to what AI means for civil servants, and differences between countries are substantial. Four clusters emerge, emphasising respectively service improvement, skills development, talent recruitment and partnerships for training. These national patterns diverge from EU-level recommendations, which put more weight on systematic upskilling. The analysis covers strategy documents, so it describes stated intentions rather than what administrations actually do.

Trade unions form coalitions with regional firms to protect employment. The authors describe visible contestation over ideas and narratives, not a single agreed direction of change. This is a single qualitative case study.

results.reader_title: Mapping how the US, China, middle powers and the EU govern AI differently
results.reader_what: Report finds jurisdictions share AI policy objectives but differ in state control and tolerance of private power.
results.reader_why: Places the EU in a shifting field where United States policy has moved towards state direction.
results.reader_more: This CERRE report offers a three-level framework for mapping AI governance geopolitically. It finds that the same broad objectives appear everywhere, including preventing harm, protecting fundamental rights, promoting innovation, industrial policy, national security and digital sovereignty, but that priorities and trade-offs differ. It then distinguishes two levers: direct control through regulation, and indirect influence over how concentrated private power is in the AI ecosystem, producing four governance postures. China combines strong state control with subordinated private firms. United States federal policy has shifted under the 2025 AI Action Plan towards asserting state influence across the technology stack, closer to the Chinese model, while some states legislate differently. Middle powers favour multilateral harmonisation. The report notes the project received input from member firms including Amazon and Microsoft.

deep_analysis.research_question: How the main jurisdictions position themselves on AI governance and what geopolitical options that leaves the EU.
deep_analysis.main_finding: AI governance regimes share objectives but diverge on state control and private power concentration, with United States federal policy moving towards state direction and middle powers defaulting to soft-law multilateralism.

deep_analysis.qualification: Analytical framework and interpretation, funded with input from large technology firms; the specific EU recommendations were not captured in the excerpt.

results.reader_title: What Europe existing tech champions suggest about innovation policy
results.reader_what: Argues European tech successes came from openness to outside innovation and early adoption, not domestic self-reliance.
results.reader_why: Cautions that economic security measures should not close off the openness that built European champions.
results.reader_more: This Centre for European Reform insight argues that Europe already has technology leaders, citing ASML, SAP, Booking.com, Spotify, Nokia and Ericsson, alongside newer firms such as Helsing, Vinted and Octopus Energy. It notes venture capital investment in European startups nearly quadrupled between 2015 and 2025 and that technology talent now flows from the United States to Europe on balance. But successes remain rare and concentrated: Europe share of global technology, media and telecommunications market capitalisation fell from 30 percent in 2000 to 7 percent in 2024. The first lesson drawn is that European champions benefited from openness to others innovation and early adoption, with ASML succeeding by building on external suppliers while a competitor tried to develop everything in-house.
